content: Since the launch of the Global Framework to Eliminate Human Rabies Transmitted by Dogs by 2030 in 2015, the World Health Organization (WHO) has collaborated with the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH), the Global Alliance for Rabies Control, and other stakeholders to develop a global strategic plan. This plan emphasizes a country-focused approach to empower and support national entities in controlling and eliminating rabies. In this context, WHO convened its network of collaborating centers, specialized institutions, members of the WHO Expert Advisory Panel on Rabies, and other experts to review and update strategic and technical guidance for rabies prevention, control, and elimination. The resulting report provides evidence-based recommendations and programmatic insights on various aspects of rabies management. Key updates include improved surveillance strategies with cross-sectoral system integration and diagnostics, updated recommendations for human and animal immunization, palliative care in resource-limited settings, risk assessment for managing bite victims, and a proposed process for validating and verifying countries achieving zero human rabies deaths. The meeting also supported recommendations from the WHO Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization (SAGE) in 2017 to enhance access to affordable rabies biologics, particularly for underserved populations, and to improve programmatic feasibility in alignment with universal health coverage goals. Collaborative mechanisms for rabies prevention serve as a model for One Health collaboration across multiple stakeholders and levels, demonstrating a successful approach to addressing zoonotic diseases. Rabies is a vaccine-preventable disease, and providing support to countries to eliminate it will alleviate the suffering it causes, particularly among children. Investing in rabies control and elimination strengthens health systems, improves equity and access to healthcare, and contributes to sustainable development. Such investments not only aim to eliminate this fatal but preventable disease but also build capacity in the world's most neglected regions. The WHO, established in 1948 as a specialized agency of the United Nations, serves as the directing and coordinating authority for international health matters. One of its core functions is to provide reliable and objective information on human health, which it fulfills through an extensive program of publications. These publications aim to support national health strategies and address pressing public health concerns globally. WHO's materials include practical manuals, internationally applicable guidelines, reviews of health policies, and consensus reports offering technical advice for decision-makers. These resources are closely aligned with WHO's priority activities, such as disease prevention, equitable health system development, and health promotion. By promoting health, preventing disease, and controlling public health threats, WHO's publications contribute to achieving its principal objective: the highest possible level of health for all people. The WHO Technical Report Series presents findings from international expert groups that provide the latest scientific and technical advice on a range of medical and public health topics. Members of these expert groups serve in their personal capacities and do not represent governments or organizations. Their views do not necessarily reflect WHO's policies or decisions. Human rabies deaths are often underreported, and the disease disproportionately affects poor and rural populations. Countries free of dog-mediated rabies, such as those in Western Europe, North America, Japan, and certain Pacific island nations, have achieved this status through sustained control efforts. However, they still incur costs for maintaining disease-free status, including surveillance and prophylaxis for travelers to endemic areas. In contrast, regions where dog rabies is endemic, such as parts of Asia, Africa, and Latin America, continue to face significant challenges in controlling the disease. Collaborative efforts and sustained commitment are essential to achieving global rabies elimination by 2030.
